blocks.text: The Turkish word for breakfast, *kahvaltı*, tells a story. It comes from *kahve altı*, roughly **before coffee**: the food you eat so as not to drink strong coffee on an empty stomach. Yet the drink of breakfast today is tea, served in the small tulip-shaped glasses of [unit 6](a1-u06-culture) and refilled again and again; coffee, if it comes, comes at the end.

A classic *kahvaltı* isn't one dish but many small ones, savoury and sweet, all on the table at once: white cheese (*beyaz peynir*) and mild yellow *kaşar*, black and green olives, tomatoes and cucumbers, butter, honey with *kaymak* (a thick clotted cream), jams, and eggs, boiled or fried with *sucuk*, a spicy sausage. There's always bread, and often a *simit*.

The simit is a ring of bread dipped in grape molasses and rolled in sesame seeds, Istanbul's breakfast on the go. Ottoman price lists record it in the city in 1525, and in the 17th century the traveller Evliya Çelebi counted 70 simit bakeries there. Sellers still walk the streets with a tray on their heads or push glass-sided carts. In İzmir the same ring is called *gevrek*.

Then there is *menemen*: eggs cooked in a small pan with tomatoes and green peppers, eaten straight from the pan with bread. Whether a real menemen has onions in it is a question that divides families and, every so often, Turkish social media.

On a weekday, breakfast is often quick: tea, some cheese and olives, a simit on the way to work. On weekends and holidays it becomes an event. Families and friends sit for hours over a *serpme kahvaltı*, a spread of dozens of little plates, and many cafés serve it all day. Some regions have breakfasts of their own. The eastern city of Van is famous for one, with herb cheese (*otlu peynir*) and *murtuğa*, a dish of flour, butter and eggs; in 2020 *Van kahvaltısı* became a registered geographical indication.

blocks.title: Kahvaltı yapmak
blocks.text: To have breakfast is *kahvaltı yapmak*: *Kahvaltı yapıyoruz* (We're having breakfast), *Kahvaltı yapıyor musun?* (Are you having breakfast?).
Here is a Sunday morning in the Turkish of this unit:

lines.tr: Simit ve peynir alıyorum. Zeytin istiyor musun?
lines.en: I'm getting simit and cheese. Do you want olives?

lines.tr: Evet, siyah zeytin istiyorum. Çayı sen mi yapıyorsun?
lines.en: Yes, I'd like black olives. Are you making the tea?

lines.tr: Hayır, çayı Ece yapıyor. Menemeni ben yapıyorum!
lines.en: No, Ece is making the tea. I'm making the menemen!

questions.explain: *Kahve altı*: the food you eat before coffee.

questions.q: What is the usual hot drink with a Turkish breakfast?
questions.explain: Tea comes glass after glass; coffee, if any, comes at the end.

questions.q: In the dialogue, who is making the tea?
questions.explain: *Çayı Ece yapıyor*: Ece is the one making the tea. The focus slot before the verb tells you.
